title: Publication 915 (2026), page 4: single, $1,500 of benefits, pension $17,000, interest $700: none taxable

source.where: Publication 915 (2026), page 4, the Worksheet A example

note: Income 17,700 + half the benefits 750 = 18,450, under the 25,000 base for single.

title: Publication 915 (2026), Example 1: single, benefits $5,980, other income $28,990: $2,990 taxable

source.where: Publication 915 (2026), page 8, Example 1 with its filled-in Worksheet 1

note: Worksheet 1 line 6 is 31,980, 6,980 over the 25,000 base; half of that is 3,490, the smaller of that and half the benefits (2,990) is taxable.

title: Publication 915 (2026), Example 2: joint, benefits $5,600, a $1,000 IRA deduction: none taxable

source.where: Publication 915 (2026), page 9, Example 2 with its filled-in Worksheet 1 (line 7)

note: Line 6 is 32,550; less the 1,000 IRA deduction, 31,550, under the 32,000 joint base, so nothing is taxable.

title: Publication 915 (2026), Example 3: joint, benefits $10,000, other income $40,500: $6,275 taxable

source.where: Publication 915 (2026), page 10, Example 3 with its filled-in Worksheet 1

note: The savings bond interest is left out, as the worksheet does: interest 2,300 + 200 = 2,500 on Schedule B line 2. Line 8 is 45,500, 1,500 over 44,000: 85% x 1,500 = 1,275 plus the smaller of 5,000 and 50% x 12,000 = 5,000, so 6,275, under 85% of the benefits (8,500).

title: Publication 915 (2026), Example 4: married filing separately, lived together, benefits $4,000: $3,400 taxable

source.where: Publication 915 (2026), page 11, Example 4 and the note on Worksheet 1 line 9
